caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1087 of 2004
lawyer:
Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali, Additional Attorney-General, instructed by Mr. B. Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ----- for the petitioners.
Mr. Md. Khurshid Alam Khan, Advocate, instructed by Mr. A.S.M. Khalequzzaman, Advocate-on-Record ----- for the Respondent.
parties:
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the DC and others ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Shamir Ghosh ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
2. Facts leading to the leave petition in short are that respondent Shamir Ghosh as plaintiff instituted other Class Suit No. 136 of 2002 before the Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar Kishoregonj seeking a declaration that Memo No. JM/420 dated 19.6.2002 issued by the Deputy Commissioner, Kishoregonj Cancelling the licence of the Universal Talkies Cinema Hall at Kishoregonj is illegal and unlawful and not binding upon him. It is stated in the plaint that the plaintiffs father rented a house in the year 1943, he obtained licence from the appropriate authority and started Cinema business. In 1966 he constructed a building for the Cinema Hall and continued the business. After the death of his father in 1980 the plaintiff was in charge of the Cinema Hall and ran it without any hindrance. On 23.8.2000 he received a notice from defendant No. 1 i.e. the Deputy Commissioner, Kishoregonj representing the Government stating that the said property is vested and non-resident property and that the plaintiff's possession is unlawful. The plaintiff prayed for lease in September, 2000 and the same having been accepted yearly lease was granted at Tk. 712/- per year. The lease money was deposited on yearly basis and thus the plaintiff complied with the terms and conditions of the lease and paid taxes up-to-date on 19.6.2000. Suddenly the impugned notice dated 19.6.2002 cancelling the lease was served upon him and hence the suit. 

 3. Having filed the suit on 25.6.2002 the plaintiff filed an application for temporary injunction pleading inter alia that he has a good prima-facie case inasmuch as the licence was cancelled purportedly under Rule 22 of the Cinematograph Rules, 1972 without as-signing any reason. The plaintiff asserted that he did not violate any of the terms and conditions of the lease. Furthermore no notice to show cause was served upon the plaintiff before cancelling the licence. 

 4. The application for injunction was contested by the defendant contending inter alia that there was a dispute between the plaintiffs landlord and his co-sharer and hence the ownership of is the land could not be ascertained and that why the licence was cancelled. However the Assistant Judge allowed the prayer for injunction restraining the opposite party from entering into the Cinema Hall and or creating any obstruction in exhibiting film in the Cinema Hall. 

 6. Having felt aggrieved the petitioner preferred Civil Revision No. 431 of 2003 before the High Court Division. On threadbare discussion the High Court Division found that though under Rule 22 of the Cinematograph Rule 1972 a licence may be revoked or suspended at any time but before cancelling the licence, reason for cancellation must be recorded. But in the instant case the reason assigned for cancellation is a dispute between landlord of the plaintiff and his co-sharer over title in the suit premises. Thus the court found that no reason has been assigned by the authority about any violation of the rules or breach of any condition and that if there is a dispute between the co-sharer of the property, they can seek relief before the appropriate forum for eviction of the tenant and that the licencing authority has nothing to do with the grievance raised by a co-sharer of the landlord of the plaintiff. The Appellate Court also made observation that the plaintiff and his predecessors had been running the Cinema Hall since 1943 and that without serving any notice to show cause the licence has been cancelled which is a clear violation of the principle of natural justice and that the balance of convenience and inconvenience is in favour of the plaintiff rather than of the defendant. 

 7. Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali, learned Additional Attorney General argued that since there was a land dispute between co-owners the High Court Division committed an error in making the rule absolute; that the lincence was cancelled for infringement of rule 22 of the Cinematograph Rules 1972 and as such the High Court Division ought to have discharged the rule, that the balance of convenience and inconvenience is in favour of the defendant petitioner and that the loss occasioned, if any, to the plaintiff is compensatable by money so injunction ought to have been refused. We find no substance and merit in the submission of the learned Additional Attorney-General and hence the petition for leave to appeal is dismissed.
